ai_summary:
**LIVE SYNTHESIS | AI GRID INSIGHTS**

Scottish wind generation is demonstrating exceptional performance at 4.4 GW, suppressing regional grid carbon intensity to an ultra-low 32 gCO₂/kWh. However, this northern generation surplus exposes severe cross-border transmission limits across the B6 Cheviot boundary. The existing network architecture is unable to evacuate these volumes southward to high-demand centres in England, resulting in 221.1 MWh of curtailed, wasted clean electricity during the current monitoring window.

To maintain transient and thermal stability across constrained interconnectors, the system operator must intervene via the Balancing Mechanism—paying northern wind assets to power down while simultaneously paying carbon-intensive generators south of the constraint to fire up. This redispatch protocol carries significant market friction; the associated constraint payments inevitably inflate Balancing Services Use of System (BSUoS) charges, transferring the economic cost of structural bottlenecks directly onto British consumers. 

While Scotland’s generation fleet proves its capacity to drive decarbonisation, real-time efficiency remains hindered by physical boundary bottlenecks. Until strategic grid upgrades and subsea HVDC bypass links achieve operational status, consumer exposure to curtailment-driven balancing costs will remain intimately correlated with high northern wind yields.
